findings.claim: Earthenware / terracotta linear coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE)
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Depends on free quartz content (alpha-beta inversion at 573 °C), firing temperature (900–1150 °C), and porosity; architectural terracotta typically 5.0–7.0 × 10^-6 /K within broader clay brick/tile range of 3.9–8.5 × 10^-6 /K.
sources: ASM Engineered Materials Handbook, Desk Edition (Sec. 22.3)

findings.claim: Earthenware / terracotta critical thermal shock delta-T (ΔTc)
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Single-event water quench tolerance for unformulated porous earthenware is generally <100 °C (<180 °F), whereas ASTM C484 / ISO 10545-9 glazed tile thermal shock cycling uses 145 ± 5 °C to 15 ± 5 °C (ΔT ≈ 130 °C / 234 °F). Per Tite et al. (2001) and Müller et al. (2014/2015), coarse-tempered porous earthenware cooking pots exhibit stable/semi-stable microcracking rather than a sharp catastrophic ΔTc collapse.
sources: Müller et al. (2014/2015), Craft and Science
findings.value_or_range: <100 °C (<180 °F) unformulated water quench; ~130 °C (234 °F) standardized tile cycle

findings.claim: Stoneware linear coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE)
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Varies with firing temperature (1200–1300 °C), glassy phase, mullite (~5.3 × 10^-6 /K), and residual quartz/cristobalite inversions (573 °C and 200–270 °C). ISO 10545-8 porcelain stoneware tile specifications span 4.1–8.1 × 10^-6 /K.
sources: ASM Engineered Materials Handbook / Ceramic Technology references

findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Standard commercial stoneware is typically limited to 100–150 °C (180–270 °F); dense vitrified porcelain/stoneware bodies in water-quench flexural tests fall in 150–250 °C (270–450 °F). ASTM C554 stepped crazing quench runs from 121 °C (250 °F) to 232 °C (450 °F) into ambient water (ΔT ≈ 100–210 °C / 180–378 °F); ASTM C484 / ISO 10545-9 cycle at ΔT ≈ 130 °C (234 °F).
sources: Ceramic materials science / Hasselmann quench literature

findings.claim: Zisha (Yixing purple clay) linear coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE)
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Peer-reviewed studies (Yang et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2013) document Zisha's quartz, mullite, cristobalite, hematite, 25–70% glass phase, and ~20% dual-pore structure, and dilatometry is used on Zisha, but the numerical 5.0–7.0 × 10^-6 /K (broader 4.0–8.0 × 10^-6 /K) range was not directly verified inside an open primary English journal abstract. High-iron/dense Zhuni (18–25% firing shrinkage) has higher sensitivity than Zini/Dicaoqing.

findings.claim: Zisha (Yixing purple clay) thermal shock failure limit / national standard ΔT
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: GB/T 10816-2008 (and updated GB/T 10816-2024, tested per GB/T 3298) mandates surviving one water-exchange shock from 180 °C to 20 °C (ΔT = 160 °C / 288 °F) without cracking; the older GB/T 10816-1989 required 200 °C to 20 °C (ΔT = 180 °C / 324 °F). Standard acceptance threshold rather than universal ultimate failure point.

findings.claim: Cordierite (flameware / technical magnesium aluminosilicate) linear CTE
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Anisotropic crystal structure (positive expansion along two axes, negative along the third) yields low bulk CTE of 1.0–3.5 × 10^-6 /K (typically 1.5–3.0 × 10^-6 /K; synthetic cordierite/spodumene flameware 2.83–3.09 × 10^-6 /K over 25–800 °C). Caveat: Corning Pyroceram Code 9606 (cordierite-rutile-cristobalite radome glass-ceramic) has higher CTE of 4.5–5.7 × 10^-6 /K.
sources: Saengchantara et al. (2012–2013) / Junlar et al. (2021), TCI journals

findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Cordierite/spodumene flameware withstands ΔT = 400 °C (720 °F) and >50 direct stovetop cycles crack-free; dense cordierite water-quench ΔTc spans 500–650 °C (900–1170 °F), with porous/microcrack-toughened honeycombs higher.
sources: Saengchantara et al. (2012–2013) / Junlar et al. (2021), TCI journals
Ceramics International / J. Eur. Ceram. Soc. cordierite quench studies

findings.claim: Petalite / Lithium Aluminosilicate (LAS) flameware & Pyroceram 9608 linear CTE
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Petalite and β-spodumene/β-eucryptite LAS ceramics exhibit near-zero or negative CTE (-0.4 to 1.7 × 10^-6 /K, typically <1.0 × 10^-6 /K). Corning Pyroceram Code 9608 (LAS cookware glass-ceramic) is 0 ± 0.3 × 10^-6 /K (0 ± 3.0 × 10^-7 /°C) across 20–700 °C. Requires matching low-CTE glazes (~2.6 × 10^-6 /K) to prevent crazing.
sources: OSTI / DOE & NIH/PubMed LAS thermal expansion studies

findings.claim: Petalite / LAS & Pyroceram 9608 critical thermal shock delta-T (ΔTc)
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Optimized LAS glass-ceramics achieve ΔTc of 500–800 °C (900–1440 °F) while retaining 80–87% flexural strength; Pyroceram 9608 is rated up to ΔTmax ≈ 700 K (700 °C / 1260 °F).

findings.claim: Gray cast iron linear CTE (ambient to moderate temperatures)
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Varies slightly with graphite flake morphology and ferritic/pearlitic matrix; rises with temperature.
sources: ASM Handbook / ASM Specialty Handbook: Cast Irons

findings.claim: Gray cast iron thermal shock failure limit (ΔT)
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Unlike brittle ceramics, cast iron has moderate thermal conductivity (40–70 W/m·K) and no single standardized ASTM ΔTc. However, flake graphite acts as internal stress raisers (E ≈ 80–140 GPa, tensile strength 98–290 MPa), so severe water quenching from elevated cooking/firing temps (400–600 °C / 752–1112 °F; ΔT of several hundred °C) or rapid cyclic heating causes brittle cracking along graphite flakes and pearlitic breakdown. Industrial cast-iron boilers limit ramp rates to 28–56 °C/h (50–100 °F/h).
sources: ASM Handbook / ASM Specialty Handbook: Cast Irons
Peer-reviewed gray cast iron cyclic water-quench thermal fatigue literature
findings.value_or_range: No single standardized ΔTc; cracking/fatigue accelerates at 400–600 °C (752–1112 °F) quench cycles

findings.claim: Aluminum (pure & wrought cookware alloys 1100, 3003, 6061) linear CTE
sources: ASM Handbook: Aluminum and Aluminum Alloys
NIST / OSTI cryogenic and thermophysical databases

findings.claim: Aluminum thermal shock failure mode and critical ΔT
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Ductile aluminum alloys have high thermal conductivity (150–230 W/m·K; 167–170 W/m·K for 6061-T6) and lower modulus (~68.9–70 GPa), so they do not suffer brittle thermal-shock shattering (no brittle ΔTc). Instead, rapid uneven heating/cooling causes plastic warping/buckling when constrained differential expansion exceeds yield strength (276 MPa at 20 °C for 6061-T6; lower for 1100/3003 and elevated temperatures).
sources: ASM Handbook: Aluminum and Aluminum Alloys
findings.value_or_range: No brittle ΔTc; fails via plastic warping/buckling when E·α·ΔT exceeds elevated-T yield strength

findings.claim: Localized burner hotspot cracking mechanism in clay cookware
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Low ceramic thermal conductivity traps heat at the burner contact patch, producing a steep spatial thermal gradient (∇T). The hot expanding core is constrained by the cooler rigid wall, generating compressive stress in the hotspot and high tensile stress at its perimeter/opposing face (σ ∝ E·α·ΔT/(1−ν)); cracks initiate when tensile stress exceeds modulus of rupture. Rounded bases mitigate sharp stress concentrations.
sources: Tite et al. (2001), Archaeometry 43(3); Müller et al. (2014/2015)
findings.value_or_range: Spatial ∇T constraint -> perimeter/opposite-face tensile stress > modulus of rupture

findings.claim: Sudden quenching (downshock) cracking mechanism in clay cookware
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Contact with cold water or a cold/wet surface drops outer skin temperature rapidly while the core remains hot and expanded. Violent surface contraction places the outer skin in immediate biaxial tension; because ceramics have high compressive strength but low tensile strength and low fracture toughness, surface microcracks propagate inward catastrophically.
findings.value_or_range: Rapid surface cooling -> surface tensile stress -> inward brittle crack propagation

findings.claim: Cold/wet clay pot in preheated oven cracking mechanism
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Combines two coupled failure drivers: (1) steep surface-to-core thermal gradient (ΔT) causing tensile thermal shock stress, and (2) internal steam pore-pressure spalling, where water trapped in porous clay capillaries flashes to steam faster than vapor can diffuse outward, raising internal gas pressure above the clay matrix's tensile strength. Cold-start ovens or dry preheating prevent both failures.
sources: University extension & ceramic cookware safety literature
findings.value_or_range: Coupled steep ∇T thermal shock + trapped-water flash-steam pore pressure spalling

findings.claim: Electric multi-cooker heating jackets & gradual PID ramps reduce thermal gradients
findings.disagreements_or_caveats: Wrap-around heating jackets/conformal bands lining a conductive inner shell distribute heat flux evenly across the lower and middle sidewalls rather than concentrating heat at a bottom disc (US Patents 2,187,888 and 6,498,323). Microcontroller PID ramp-and-soak profiles replace binary bang-bang bimetallic thermostats (US Patents 6,573,483; 6,740,855; 10,588,443), capping dT/dt and damping thermal-lag overshoot so heat diffuses uniformly through low-conductivity clay walls before destructive ΔT gradients form.
sources: US Patent No. 2,187,888 (Naxon, si.edu) & US Patent No. 6,498,323 (Rival)
US Patent Nos. 6,573,483, 6,740,855, and 10,588,443; industrial ceramic PID control literature
findings.value_or_range: Conformal sidewall heat distribution + rate-limited PWM PID ramp-soak eliminating overshoot and steep ∇T

myths_checked: Soaking a clay pot in water protects it in a preheated oven -> FALSE: pore-trapped water flashes to steam inside a preheated oven, adding internal vapor-pressure spalling to thermal shock; soaked pots must start in a cold oven.

Denser high-fired stoneware/porcelain always survives stovetop thermal shock better than porous low-fired earthenware -> FALSE/NUANCED: while stronger mechanically, dense vitrified bodies fail abruptly once ΔTc is exceeded unless low-CTE phases (cordierite/petalite) are used, whereas coarse-tempered porous earthenware arrests cracks and undergoes gradual damage accumulation (Tite et al., 2001; Müller et al., 2014).

Metal cookware cannot fail from thermal shock -> FALSE: gray cast iron can brittle-crack along flake graphite stress raisers under severe quenching, while ductile aluminum yields plastically and warps/buckles from uneven rapid heating/cooling due to its high CTE (~23 × 10^-6 /K).

All Corning Pyroceram grades have near-zero thermal expansion -> FALSE: Pyroceram Code 9608 (LAS cookware) has ~0 ± 0.3 × 10^-6 /K CTE, whereas Pyroceram Code 9606 (cordierite missile radome glass-ceramic) has 4.5–5.7 × 10^-6 /K CTE (Corning / NIST).
